_how_to_edit: The story page, replay map and home hero read this file on every load. Edit it, run `node groundstop/src/build.js`, commit and push to main; no Squarespace edit is needed. Times are hours on an Eastern clock on Nov. 13, 2026 (17.5 = 5:30 p.m.; values past 24 mean Nov. 14). Set lift to null while the stop is in effect.
headline_status: The FAA lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. Eastern, after more than four hours
cause: Telecommunications outage on older FAA hardware
moments: A Friday afternoon, with flights departing on schedule across the country.
About 3:10 p.m.
Flights bound for Chicago O’Hare are stopped over communications problems, and Midway follows three minutes later.
Radar and communications at centers and approach facilities across the country become unstable, the transportation secretary says later.
Nationwide ground stop. More than 3,100 flights already in the air are allowed to continue to their destinations.
The transportation secretary says a communication issue is affecting air route traffic control centers.
The FAA advisory now runs to 11:30 p.m. Eastern, and no end time is confirmed.
About 5:15 p.m.
The FAA says a temporary telecommunications outage caused the stop, and officials say they see no sign of an attack.
About 6:00 p.m.
The FAA says the stop remains in effect and that flights will be released as each en route center recovers.
Fox Weather counts 598 commercial flights still in the air, down from more than 3,100 when the stop began.
About 7:10 p.m.
An airline source tells CNN that major airlines could shut down operations for the rest of the night.
FlightAware counts 5,117 cancellations and 9,814 delays, and JetBlue and United call off most of their remaining Friday flights.
The airspace reopens, the transportation secretary says, about 4 hours and 21 minutes after the nationwide stop began.
By 8:48 p.m.
At a White House briefing, the transportation secretary says older hardware failed and that none of the FAA’s new systems went down.
facts: Eastern start time, the only one of the three stops to begin after noon
flights in the air when the stop began, allowed to finish their trips
length of the stop, against about 90 minutes in 2023, with more than 9,100 Friday flights canceled in FlightAware’s count as of Saturday morning
unknown: What is not known. The airspace reopened at 8:15 p.m. Eastern, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a White House briefing on Friday night, according to the Department of Transportation. Duffy said switches and routers on older hardware were overloaded with data, beginning at 3:36 p.m., and Trump administration officials said new technology being added to the air traffic control system overloaded the older equipment, according to the Associated Press. Officials have not named that technology or said where the failure began. Three days earlier, on Nov. 10, the agency expanded SMART, an AI tool that suggests flight reroutes, to all 22 centers. Duffy said SMART is not connected to the equipment that failed, according to the Department of Transportation, and the tool’s contractor said the stop was not a result of SMART, according to ABC News.
status_html: The FAA lifted the stop at 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Friday, about 4 hours and 21 minutes after it began. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy gave the time at a White House briefing, saying, “At 8:15 tonight, Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” according to the Department of Transportation. Flying will take longer to recover than the stop took to end, because JetBlue canceled all of its remaining Friday flights except Europe-bound departures from New York and Boston, United said it would cancel most of its remaining flights for the night, and Air Canada canceled the rest of its Friday flights to and from the United States. After the stop was lifted, United said it was “resuming operations, including some planned Friday night flights,” according to ABC News. FlightAware had counted 5,117 cancellations and 9,814 delays by 8 p.m., according to CNN, which is about twice the 2,500 cancellations counted at 6:30 p.m. More than 700 Saturday flights were already canceled by 7:45 p.m., and the data firm Cirium estimated that 1.5 million people were stranded. The totals kept growing overnight. FlightAware counted 9,138 cancellations of U.S. flights on Friday, according to Men’s Journal in an article published at 6:57 a.m. Eastern on Saturday, and Fox Weather, in an article published at 6:42 a.m., cited FlightAware for more than 9,100, which is about seven times the 1,300-plus cancellations logged on the day of the 2023 stop. The reports disagree on Friday’s delays, with Men’s Journal giving 7,068 and Fox Weather more than 24,500, both attributed to FlightAware, against the 9,814 that CNN reported at 8 p.m., so this page does not give a final delay count. For Saturday, FlightAware listed more than 3,400 canceled flights within, into or out of the United States by Saturday morning and 1,111 delays as of 6:45 a.m. Eastern, according to Men’s Journal, up from the roughly 2,650 Saturday cancellations that Euronews reported at about 1:55 a.m. and from more than 700 at 7:45 p.m. on Friday. The Associated Press, in a report published at 7:20 a.m. Eastern on Saturday, gave a lower figure of more than 2,500 flights canceled in the U.S. on Saturday, also citing FlightAware and without a time for the count, so the early reports of Saturday’s cancellations ranged from more than 2,500 to more than 3,400. The count kept rising through the morning, and by 9:10 a.m. Eastern FlightAware listed more than 3,600 canceled flights within, into or out of the United States on Saturday and more than 1,800 delays, according to Yahoo News. ABC13 in Houston, also citing FlightAware, reported more than 3,600 cancellations and more than 1,600 delays as of Saturday morning without giving a time, so this page gives Saturday’s delays as more than 1,600. The airspace was operating normally by 7:30 a.m. Eastern on Saturday, according to Yahoo News, which cited CBS News. Delta had canceled 629 Saturday flights, or 20% of its schedule, and JetBlue 335, or 40% of its schedule, as of 6:45 a.m., according to the same report. The FAA said that before clearing flights to resume it “thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable,” according to Euronews. Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at a White House briefing on Friday night that schedules would take a while to recover, with most planes likely to get going on Saturday morning, according to Deadline. Officials said the system is likely to be operating normally in time for the Thanksgiving travel rush, according to the AP.
compare_html: Friday's stop lasted about 261 minutes, close to three times the roughly 90 minutes of 2023, and it began late on a Friday afternoon where the 2023 stop began early on a Wednesday, which left airlines almost none of the day to recover. The more than 9,100 Friday cancellations that FlightAware counted, as reported by Fox Weather and Men’s Journal on Saturday morning, were about seven times the 1,300-plus logged for the whole day in 2023, while reports of Friday’s delays range from 7,068 to more than 24,500 against that day's roughly 10,000. Cirium counted 26,284 flights scheduled to depart the United States on Friday and said more than 15% were canceled or never took off, and at least 827 flights were diverted, 670 of them back to the airport they left. The effects reach into Saturday: the Big 12 told CNN it is evaluating changes to its football schedule because teams could not travel.
notknown_html:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy gave the first official account of the cause at a White House briefing on Friday night. ABC News reported that he blamed overloaded routers, and Deadline quoted him describing a radar “instability” problem and saying, “It was the old hardware that went down,” and that “none of the new systems went down.” Duffy said the instability in radar and communications began at 3:36 p.m. Eastern, 18 minutes before the nationwide stop, according to the Department of Transportation’s account of the briefing. Trump administration officials said that new technology being added to the air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” gaps in communications and radar, according to the Associated Press, which did not name the officials or the technology. Duffy said, “This is all the old legacy equipment. All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down,” and he warned that “you will have more of these,” according to the AP. Officials have not said which technology overloaded the routers, where the failure began or why it spread to all 22 centers.

Several accounts go further than officials have. An airline source told CNN that the FAA told airlines the outages resulted from a problem with network routers, and that the problem is believed to have started at Chicago Midway and spread nationwide. CBS News reported that an update to the private communications network linking air traffic control facilities caused the system to reboot, and that the network is operated by the contractor L3Harris, which had not responded to its request for comment. The FAA has confirmed none of these details.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a threat to the country, and the FAA said it does not believe the outage was a cyberattack. Mullin said at the briefing that officials had seen “zero evidence” of a cyberattack, according to Deadline, which reported that he would not rule one out. A senior security source told CNN late Friday that the FBI, the Department of Homeland Security and the National Security Agency had found no sign of an attack and that the search of the aviation system’s network connections would continue for days.

Three days before the stop, on Nov. 10, the FAA expanded SMART, an AI tool that suggests flight reroutes, to all 22 centers. Mullin said the administration is examining that rollout, according to Fox News. Duffy said at the briefing that SMART “is completely disconnected” from the equipment that failed and that “there’s no possible way SMART would have impacted what happened,” according to the Department of Transportation. The tool’s contractor said in a statement that the ground stop “is not based on or a result of the SMART system,” according to ABC News, and no official or major outlet has reported a link. The AP reported early Saturday that Duffy said the problems were not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system, and its report does not identify the new technology that officials said overloaded the older equipment.

This story reflects what was known at 10:03 a.m. Eastern on Nov. 14, 2026. The lift time is the one Duffy gave at the briefing, and we will update the cause and the final delay and cancellation counts as the FAA and flight trackers report them.
